newsitem.title: EGYPT: Foreign fund inflows push up Egyptian pound.
newsitem.headline: Foreign fund inflows push up Egyptian pound.

text.p: The Egyptian pound has appreciated against the dollar on the back of large foreign inflows into the Egyptian pound money market, bankers said on Monday.
The Central Bank and public-sector banks have not intervened on a large scale to prevent the pound's appreciation, despite a government commitment to exchange rate stability, they added.

The appreciation is minor by the standards of international currency markets -- about one quarter of a percent in the past week -- but it is probably the fastest movement the pound has seen since the government floated the currency six years ago.
The Central Bank said the average spot rate at midday on Monday stood at about 3.395 pounds to the dollar, against the longstanding average of about 3.40 pounds.
But the most active trading rooms said the real appreciation was greater, as much as one piastre (0.01 pounds) to the dollar.
"There are lots of dollars coming in from abroad. In one month we alone have had $150 million to $200 million coming into treasury bills and pound time deposits," one banker said.

Investors are also switching from dollars to pounds to join the Egyptian stock market bandwagon, where the all-share index has risen 41 percent since the beginning of the year. The close on Sunday was the 19th straight record high.
"We have had to press the public-sector banks really hard to take the dollars off us. No one else would take them. The dollar was really oversold," the banker added.
The four big public-sector banks act as a channel between the private-sector banks and the secretive Central Bank, which rarely makes public statements on exchange rate policy.

Central Bank officials declined to comment on Monday on how the bank planned to handle the dollar surplus. The bank has already accumulated foreign currency reserves of about $19 billion, enough for more than 14 months of imports.
The incentive to buy pounds, as in the past, is the large differential between dollar and Egyptian pound interest rates, coupled with expectations that the pound will not lose value.
The average yield on Egyptian treasury bills has fallen slowly but remains a fraction under 10 percent. Six-month deposits in banks can earn more than nine percent.
"Now that the pound is rising, there's a double incentive to move into pounds. You gain both ways," one banker said.
Another incentive is the investment-grade rating assigned by Standard and Poor's last month, widely seen as a clean bill of health for the Egyptian money markets.

"There's big demand from banks in England and in Arab countries. They come to us with dollars for pounds, asking for treasury bills. Others are transferring the money to brokers to buy shares," said another banker.
The bankers said that as buyer of last resort the Central Bank would have to absorb the inflows and that its best option would be to bring Egyptian pound interest rates down faster.
"I can't see why they (the Central Bank) are sticking at 10 percent (on treasury bills). The 10 percent psychological barrier has already been broken anyway," one of them said.
But another banker noted that a sudden fall in interest rates would have the side-effect of adding fire to the flames of the stock market boom, which the government may not welcome.
"They can't let interest rates go down until the stock market cools off," he added.
"I expect the dollar to keep going down against the pound, because I see the inflows continuing as long as interest rates stay at this level," he said.
$1 = 3.395 pounds
